cim: GP Resident Doctors Use Generative AI for Administration While Navigating Clinical Risks

szoveg_eredeti:
GP Resident Doctors Use Generative AI for Administration While Navigating Clinical Risks

General practice resident doctors are employing generative artificial intelligence to mitigate administrative workloads and assist their educational training, while underscoring that professional accountability and clinical judgement must remain strictly with physicians. Findings from a newly published qualitative investigation show that these resident clinicians, who balance simultaneous responsibilities as medical learners and practicing doctors, view automated tools as valuable aids for routine documentation and learning support but maintain significant reservations regarding accuracy, data confidentiality, and skill preservation.

The study highlights that while the integration of generative artificial intelligence has expanded across broader healthcare environments, relatively little empirical research had previously documented how general practice resident doctors navigate these emerging technologies in day-to-day settings. Because general practice trainees occupy an unusual position that requires developing independent diagnostic competence while managing substantial clinical care, their direct encounters provide a unique perspective on the intersection of automated computational tools and early-career professional development.

To investigate these perspectives, researchers designed a qualitative inquiry situated within a post-positivist research paradigm. The project specifically examined how resident doctors in general practice currently incorporate generative artificial intelligence into their professional routines, while capturing their direct evaluations of the associated benefits, hazards, and existing educational requirements necessary to practice safely in digital healthcare environments.

Methodologically, the investigative team conducted five semi-structured focus groups with a total of sixteen general practice resident doctors recruited from the Northern region. The resulting qualitative dataset was systematically reviewed using thematic analysis, which identified four overarching thematic domains: artificial intelligence as a response to workload and time pressure, artificial intelligence as a clinical cognitive aid and educational support, safe use requiring professional judgement and accountability, and preparing for an artificial intelligence-enabled future.

According to the analyzed focus group accounts, participants routinely applied generative artificial intelligence to improve operational efficiency when handling repetitive, administration-heavy duties. Trainees highlighted using these tools to streamline clinical documentation, draft written professional communications, and facilitate portfolio development. Beyond administrative relief, participants described generative systems as cognitive aids that assisted clinical reasoning and educational preparation by delivering personalized informational outputs and significantly decreasing the time required to compile study materials.

Alongside operational benefits, the resident doctors articulated serious concerns surrounding factual accuracy, patient confidentiality, and the potential loss of fundamental clinical competencies caused by over-reliance on automated systems. Participants reported mitigating these hazards by actively verifying artificial intelligence outputs and avoiding uncritical dependence, concluding that current inconsistencies in formal training necessitate clearer institutional guidance to help developing general practitioners balance technological efficiency against emerging clinical risks.

The authors emphasized that generative artificial intelligence should supplement rather than replace clinical expertise, with full responsibility for patient care remaining with the doctor. By focusing specifically on general practice resident doctors, the investigation provides insight into how clinicians who are still developing their skills and professional judgement perceive and navigate the introduction of these tools into routine clinical practice. The findings reinforce that although generative systems assist clinical reasoning and learning, personal clinical expertise must remain central to medical decision making.

In addition, the reported experiences highlight clear inconsistencies in current artificial intelligence training available to these trainees. As the operational role of generative artificial intelligence continues to expand across everyday healthcare settings, the researchers underscored an urgent requirement for clearer institutional guidance. Clearer educational standards are necessary to help resident doctors effectively balance the practical benefits of generative systems against emerging clinical and professional risks encountered throughout their ongoing general practice training.

Subject of Research: Generative artificial intelligence adoption and perceptions in postgraduate general practice training

Article Title: Exploring the use of generative AI in postgraduate GP training: a qualitative study of resident doctors’ experiences and perceptions

Article References: Tankard, G., Dong, J., Alberti, H., Redford, S., Punchayil, S., & Anderson, A. (2026). Exploring the use of generative AI in postgraduate GP training: a qualitative study of resident doctors’ experiences and perceptions. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-10938-9

Keywords: generative artificial intelligence, general practice, resident doctors, postgraduate training, medical education, clinical practice, qualitative study, focus groups, thematic analysis, administrative burden, clinical reasoning, documentation, portfolio development, patient confidentiality, professional judgement, clinical skills
